messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Mateo, a 35-year-old Latin American guitarist and vocalist, was driving home from a late-night rehearsal in east Los Angeles when a pickup truck ran a red light and slammed into his driver’s-side door at nearly sixty miles per hour. He remembers the glass shattering, the metal folding inward around his ribs, and the sound of his own voice screaming before everything went black. Emergency responders cut him out of the wreckage; he spent three days in intensive care with a collapsed lung, a fractured pelvis, and internal bleeding. He was told he was minutes from dying. In the months after the accident, Mateo’s memory of the collision remained stubbornly out of reach. When he tried to reconstruct what happened, he could only access disconnected fragments—the glare of headlights, the smell of gasoline, the cold of the hydraulic cutters against his hip—that refused to form a coherent timeline. He felt as though he was only remembering pieces of the story while the core of the event stayed hidden.

What Mateo could recall with sharp clarity was the aftermath: the driver had no insurance and faced only a minor citation; the case was closed within weeks. This injustice burrowed into him. He began to believe that his life had been destroyed in that intersection—not just his body, but his future as a musician, his sense of safety, his belief in any kind of fairness. And when the anger rose, it came with a frightening intensity. He was terrified that he would lose control, that the rage would spill out in a way he could not take back. Because he feared that loss of control, he started to avoid any situation that might trigger that anger. He stopped talking about the accident altogether, changing the subject whenever a bandmate asked how he was healing. He also began to keep himself constantly surrounded by people—after every gig, he insisted on going out with the whole crew, staying up late at bars or at someone’s apartment, never letting the conversation quiet down long enough for his own thoughts to surface. The constant socializing drained him, but it felt safer than being alone with the fragments of what happened.

The gaps in his memory only deepened his sense of injustice. If he could not even hold the full picture of the crash, how could anyone hold the driver accountable? The incomplete picture became proof that the system had failed him, that his story could never be fully told. At the same time, his belief that his life was destroyed made him deliberately avoid thinking about the event, which in turn made the memory even harder to retrieve deliberately. The less he tried to recall, the more disjointed the fragments became. And the constant socializing—meant to keep the thoughts at bay—actually worsened the fragmentation. By never giving himself a quiet moment to mentally piece the events together, he was actively preventing his memory from cohering.

At home, his wife began to notice that he would not sit still. Even on his days off, he invited other musicians over, or he went to open-mic nights just to be in a crowd. He refused to drive past the intersection where the accident happened, though he never said why. The only time he was alone was in the shower, and there the fragments would flood in uninvited. He would freeze under the water, heart racing, unable to move until the hot water ran cold. His playing suffered—he was distracted during rehearsals, his timing off, his lyrics suddenly full of images he did not mean to write. He started cancelling solo shows because the thought of standing on stage alone, with only his guitar and his thoughts, felt unbearable.

What finally brought Mateo to seek help was the night he opened a kitchen drawer and stared at a steak knife for a long moment, not wanting to hurt himself but terrified by the impulse to break something—anything—that might release the pressure inside him. His wife found him there and insisted he call a therapist the next morning. Now, sitting in the waiting room, he is most afraid that if he stops avoiding, if he lets himself remember the whole thing, he might finally crack open and never stop being angry. He hopes, quietly, that someone can help him find the pieces he has lost, and that the picture they make is not as broken as it feels.
